<system-reminder>
## Swarm Mode

You are now in "agent swarm" mode. The user may send tasks that require a large number of parallel subagents.

## Workflow

You do not need to use TodoList to record this workflow.

1. First, you may need to do a small amount of exploratory work before deciding how to divide the task across subagents. You may not need subagents during this exploratory phase.

2. After exploring, if you are convinced no subagent is needed to complete the task, tell the user why and wait for further instructions; otherwise, continue with the appropriate delegation.

3. Once you have enough context, do not handle the main work yourself. Use AgentSwarm with a `prompt_template` containing the `{{item}}` placeholder and an `items` array for the requested or appropriate number of subagents, partitioning the problem so each item gives one subagent a distinct part of the work. Pass `subagent_type` when the whole swarm should use a non-default subagent profile.

## Coordination

- Give each subagent a distinct scope of work.
- Avoid duplicating work across subagents.
- Avoid assigning conflicting changes or responsibilities to different subagents.
- Remember that subagents have your full capabilities. Do not overload their prompts with excessive detail; only describe the necessary background and each subagent's specific task.
- Unless the user explicitly specifies a lower limit, do not try to conserve the number of agents. AgentSwarm supports up to 128 subagents and queues launches automatically, so decompose work as finely as possible while keeping subagent responsibilities non-conflicting; combine tasks only when they are genuinely inseparable. If the subagents only need to read, inspect, or report back without making changes, their scopes may overlap slightly.
</system-reminder>

payload.prompt:
You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this - finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool - does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only - your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

1 ## Atlas: manage your database schema as code 2 3 [![Twitter](https://img.shields.io/twitter/url.svg?label=Follow%20%40ariga%2Fatlas&style=social&url=https%3A%2F%2Ftwitter.com%2Fatlasgo_io)](https://twitter.com/atlasgo_io) 4 [![Discord](https://img.shields.io/discord/930720389120794674?label=discord&logo=discord&style=flat-square&logoColor=white)](https://discord.com/invite/zZ6sWVg6NT) 5 6

7 8 9 10

11 12 Atlas is a language-agnostic tool for managing and migrating database schemas using modern DevOps principles. 13 It offers two workflows: 14 15 - **Declarative**: Similar to Terraform, Atlas compares the current state of the database to the desired state, as 16 defined in an [HCL], [SQL], or [ORM] schema. Based on this comparison, it generates and executes a migration plan to 17 transition the database to its desired state. 18 19 - **Versioned**: Unlike other tools, Atlas automatically plans schema migrations for you. Users can describe their desired 20 database schema in [HCL], [SQL], or their chosen [ORM], and by utilizing Atlas, they can plan, lint, and apply the 21 necessary migrations to the database. 22 23 ## Quick installation 24 25 **macOS + Linux:** 26 27 ```bash 28 curl -sSf https://atlasgo.sh | sh 29 ``` 30 31 **Homebrew:** 32 33 ```bash 34 brew install ariga/tap/atlas 35 ``` 36 37 **Docker:** 38 39 ```bash 40 docker pull arigaio/atlas 41 ``` 42 43 **NPM:** 44 45 ```bash 46 npx @ariga/atlas 47 ``` 48 49 Click [here](https://atlasgo.io/getting-started#installation) to read instructions for other platforms. 50 51 ## Getting started 52 Get started with Atlas by following the [Getting Started](https://atlasgo.io/getting-started/) docs. 53 This tutorial teaches you how to inspect a database, generate a migration plan and apply the migration to your database. 54 55 ## Key features: 56 57 - **Schema management**: The `atlas schema` command offers various options for inspecting, diffing, comparing, and modifying 58 database schemas. 59 - **Versioned migration**: The `atlas migrate` command provides a state-of-the-art experience for planning, linting, and 60 applying migrations. 61 - **Terraform support**: Managing database changes as part of a Terraform deployment workflow. 62 - **[SQL], [HCL] and [ORM] support**: Atlas enables users to define their desired database schema using [HCL], [SQL], or their chosen [ORM]. 63 - **Multi-tenancy**: Atlas includes built-in support for multi-tenant database schemas. 64 - **Cloud integration**: Atlas integrates with standard cloud services and provides an easy way to read secrets from cloud 65 providers such as AWS Secrets Manager and GCP Secret Manager. 66 67 ## `schema inspect` 68 _**Easily inspect your database schema by providing a database URL and convert it to HCL, JSON, SQL, ERD, or other formats.**_ 69 70 Inspect a specific MySQL schema and get its representation in Atlas DDL syntax: 71 ```shell 72 atlas schema inspect -u "mysql://root:pass@localhost:3306/example" > schema.hcl 73 ``` 74 75
Result 76 77 ```hcl 78 table "users" { 79 schema = schema.example 80 column "id" { 81 null = false 82 type = int 83 } 84 ... 85 } 86 ``` 87
88 89 Inspect the entire MySQL database and get its JSON representation: 90 ```shell 91 atlas schema inspect \ 92 --url "mysql://root:pass@localhost:3306/" \ 93 --format '{{ json . }}' | jq 94 ``` 95 96
Result 97 98 ```json 99 { 100 "schemas": [ 101 { 102 "name": "example", 103 "tables": [ 104 { 105 "name": "users", 106 "columns": [ 107 ... 108 ] 109 } 110 ] 111 } 112 ] 113 } 114 ``` 115
116 117 Inspect a specific PostgreSQL schema and get its representation in SQL DDL syntax: 118 ```shell 119 atlas schema inspect \ 120 --url "postgres://root:pass@:5432/test?search_path=public&sslmode=disable" \ 121 --format '{{ sql . }}' 122 ``` 123 124
Result 125 126 ```sql 127 -- create "users" table 128 CREATE TABLE "users" ("id" integer NULL, ...); 129 -- create "posts" table 130 CREATE TABLE "posts" ("id" integer NULL, ...); 131 ``` 132
133 134 Inspect a specific PostgreSQL schema and get its ERD representation in the browser: 135 ```shell 136 atlas schema inspect \ 137 --url "postgres://root:pass@:5432/test?search_path=public&sslmode=disable" \ 138 -w 139 ``` 140 141 [![ERD](https://atlasgo.io/uploads/erd-example.png)](https://gh.atlasgo.cloud/explore/40d83919) 142 143 144 Inspect a specific PostgreSQL schema and get its ERD representation Mermaid syntax: 145 ```shell 146 atlas schema inspect \ 147 --url "postgres://root:pass@:5432/test?search_path=public&sslmode=disable" \ 148 --format '{{ mermaid . }}' 149 ``` 150 151 ```mermaid 152 erDiagram 153 users { 154 int id PK 155 varchar name 156 } 157 blog_posts { 158 int id PK 159 varchar title 160 text body 161 int author_id FK 162 } 163 blog_posts }o--o| users : author_fk 164 ``` 165 166 ## `schema diff` 167 _**Compare two schema states and get a migration plan to transform one into the other. A state can be specified using a 168 database URL, HCL or SQL schema, or a migration directory.**_ 169 170 Compare two MySQL schemas: 171 ```shell 172 atlas schema diff \ 173 --from mysql://root:pass@:3306/db1 \ 174 --to mysql://root:pass@:3306/db2 175 ``` 176 177
Result 178 179 ```sql 180 -- Drop "users" table 181 DROP TABLE `users`; 182 ``` 183
184 185 Compare a MySQL schema with a migration directory: 186 ```shell 187 atlas schema diff \ 188 --from mysql://root:pass@:3306/db1 \ 189 --to file://migrations \ 190 --dev-url docker://mysql/8/db1 191 ```` 192 193 Compare a PostgreSQL schema with an Atlas schema in HCL format: 194 ```shell 195 atlas schema diff \ 196 --from "postgres://postgres:pass@:5432/test?search_path=public&sslmode=disable" \ 197 --to file://schema.hcl \ 198 --dev-url "docker://postgres/15/test" 199 ```` 200 201 Compare an HCL schema with an SQL schema: 202 ```shell 203 atlas schema diff \ 204 --from file://schema.sql \ 205 --to file://schema.hcl \ 206 --dev-url docker://postgres/15/test 207 ```` 208 209 ## `schema apply` 210 _**Generate a migration plan and apply it to the database to bring it to the desired state. The desired state can be 211 specified using a database URL, HCL or SQL schema, or a migration directory.**_ 212 213 Update the database to the state defined in the HCL schema: 214 ```shell 215 atlas schema apply \ 216 --url mysql://root:pass@:3306/db1 \ 217 --to file://schema.hcl \ 218 --dev-url docker://mysql/8/db1 219 ``` 220 221
Result 222 223 ```shell 224 -- Planned Changes: 225 -- Modify "users" table 226 ALTER TABLE `db1`.`users` DROP COLUMN `d`, ADD COLUMN `c` int NOT NULL; 227 Use the arrow keys to navigate: ↓ ↑ → ← 228 ? Are you sure?: 229 ▸ Apply 230 Abort 231 ``` 232
233 234 Update the database to the state defined in a specific version of the migration directory: 235 ```shell 236 atlas schema apply \ 237 --url mysql://root:pass@:3306/db1 \ 238 --to "file://migrations?version=20221118091226" \ 239 --dev-url docker://mysql/8/db1 240 ``` 241 242 ### Additional `schema` commands 243 Atlas offers additional commands to assist users managing their database schemas. These include `schema clean` and 244 `schema fmt`. For more information, see the versioned migration documentation at https://atlasgo.io/declarative/inspect. 245 246 ## `migrate diff` 247 _**Write a new migration file to the migration directory that bring it to the desired state. The desired state can be 248 specified using a database URL, HCL or SQL schema, or a migration directory.**_ 249 250 Create a migration file named `add_blog_posts` in the migration directory to bring the database to the state defined 251 in an HCL schema: 252 ```shell 253 atlas migrate diff add_blog_posts \ 254 --dir file://migrations \ 255 --to file://schema.hcl \ 256 --dev-url docker://mysql/8/test 257 ``` 258 259 Create a migration file named `add_blog_posts` in the migration directory to bring the database to the state defined 260 in an SQL schema: 261 ```shell 262 atlas migrate diff add_blog_posts \ 263 --dir file://migrations \ 264 --to file://schema.sql \ 265 --dev-url docker://mysql/8/test 266 ``` 267 268 Create a migration file named `add_blog_posts` in the migration directory to bring the database to the state defined 269 by another database: 270 ```shell 271 atlas migrate diff add_blog_posts \ 272 --dir file://migrations \ 273 --to mysql://root:pass@host:3306/db \ 274 --dev-url docker://mysql/8/test 275 ``` 276 277 ## `migrate apply` 278 _**Apply all or part of pending migration files in the migration directory on the database.**_ 279 280 Apply all pending migration files in the migration directory on a MySQL database: 281 ```shell 282 atlas migrate apply \ 283 --url mysql://root:pass@:3306/db1 \ 284 --dir file://migrations 285 ``` 286 287 Apply in **dry run** mode the first the pending migration file in the migration directory on a PostgreSQL schema: 288 ```shell 289 atlas migrate apply \ 290 --url "postgres://root:pass@:5432/test?search_path=public&sslmode=disable" \ 291 --dir file://migrations \ 292 --dry-run 293 ``` 294 295 ### Additional `migrate` commands 296 Atlas offers additional commands to assist users managing their database migrations. These include `migrate lint`, 297 `migrate status`, and more. For more information, see the versioned migration documentation at https://atlasgo.io/versioned/diff. 298 299 ### Supported databases 300 MySQL, MariaDB, PostgresSQL, SQLite, TiDB, CockroachDB, SQL Server, ClickHouse, Redshift. 301 302 ## Supported Version Policy 303 304 To ensure the best performance, security and compatibility with the Atlas Cloud service, the Atlas team 305 will only support the two most recent minor versions of the CLI. For example, if the latest version is 306 `v0.25`, the supported versions will be `v0.24` and `v0.25` (in addition to any patch releases and the 307 "canary" release which is built twice a day). 308 309 ### Old Binaries 310 311 As part of the *Supported Version Policy* mentioned above, binaries for versions that were published 312 more than 6 months ago will be removed from the CDN and Docker Hub. 313 314 [HCL]: https://atlasgo.io/atlas-schema/hcl 315 [SQL]: https://atlasgo.io/atlas-schema/sql 316 [ORM]: https://atlasgo.io/orms

Probe `schema fmt --help` verbatim; then exhaustively: `schema fmt` with no args (in a dir with and without .hcl files); `schema fmt file.hcl` on /workspace/assets/formatted.hcl and /workspace/assets/unformatted.hcl (does it print or rewrite in place? compare file before/after, diff against formatted.hcl); multiple file args; `schema fmt -` or stdin piping if supported; nonexistent file; malformed HCL (assets/malformed_config.hcl); directory argument; formatting of comments, weird spacing, inline comments, lists, function calls, heredocs if any. Note the community-edition notice: which stream, when exactly it appears, and whether it appears for every command or only some.

SCHEMA APPLY. Spec file: /workspace/specs/schema_apply.md. `schema apply --help` verbatim. Probe against fresh sqlite files: apply an HCL schema file (use /workspace/assets/formatted.hcl as --to file://...) with --dev-url if required; `--dry-run`; `--auto-approve`; default behavior when stdin is not a TTY (does it prompt? error? auto-abort?); feed 'y'/newline via stdin and via pseudo-TTY (`script -qec`); apply SQL file as --to; apply when already in sync (no changes output); error cases (bad --to file, missing url). Record the exact plan output format ('-- Planned Changes:' etc.), prompts, exit codes, and what actually lands in the sqlite db (verify with python3 sqlite3 .schema).

SCHEMA DIFF. Spec file: /workspace/specs/schema_diff.md. `schema diff --help` verbatim. Probe diffs between: two sqlite files (empty vs with tables); sqlite vs HCL file (does it need --dev-url? try --dev-url 'sqlite://dev?mode=memory'); HCL vs HCL; covering change kinds: add table, drop table, add column, drop column, modify column type/null/default, add/drop index, add/drop PK, add/drop FK, rename?. Record exact SQL output format (comments like '-- Add "users" table', statement text, semicolons, ordering of statements) for sqlite dialect. Error cases: missing --from/--to, identical schemas (empty diff output/exit code?).

SCHEMA CLEAN. Spec file: /workspace/specs/schema_clean.md. `schema clean --help` verbatim. Probe on sqlite db containing tables/indexes/views: default behavior (prompt? abort when non-TTY?), `--auto-approve`, `--dry-run` if it exists, exact output messages, exit codes, verification that objects were dropped, behavior on already-empty db.

MIGRATE NEW/HASH/VALIDATE. Spec file: /workspace/specs/migrate_dir.md. Probe `migrate new --help`, `migrate hash --help`, `migrate validate --help` verbatim. In scratch dirs: `migrate new` (file naming — is it timestamped? deterministic parts?), `migrate new myname`, `--dir` flag variants (file://migrations, plain path); then hand-write migration files and run `migrate hash` — capture the EXACT bytes of the generated atlas.sum (hex/base64? format per line) and how it changes with file contents, order, and edits; `migrate validate` on valid dir, on tampered file (checksum error exact text), on missing atlas.sum, on directory with non-.sql files; `migrate hash` on empty dir. Everything about atlas.sum format is critical — record full examples with the exact file contents you used so the hashing scheme can be reverse-engineered (try to figure out the hash algorithm: test if lines are base64 of hmac/sha256 of name+content etc.; you may compute candidate hashes with python3 hashlib/hmac and compare — that is allowed since it is your own analysis of outputs).

MIGRATE APPLY/STATUS/SET. Spec file: /workspace/specs/migrate_apply.md. Probe `--help` verbatim for `migrate apply`, `migrate status`, `migrate set`. Using sqlite URLs and file:// migration dirs you create: `migrate status` on fresh db + empty dir, fresh db + migrations, applied db; `migrate apply` with --dry-run and for real (record exact log output, revision table created — inspect db with python3 to see atlas_schema_revisions contents/structure); applying 1 vs N pending files; `migrate apply 1` (count arg?) if supported; dirty state behavior (make a migration fail midway — e.g. bad SQL — then status/apply again, exact error texts); `migrate set` usage and output; checksum mismatch errors; `--baseline`, `--tx-mode`, `--allow-dirty` flags if present. Record exact stdout/stderr/exit codes.

MIGRATE DIFF/LINT/IMPORT. Spec file: /workspace/specs/migrate_diff.md. Probe `--help` verbatim for `migrate diff`, `migrate lint`, `migrate import`. Try `migrate diff name --dir file://migrations --to file://schema.hcl --dev-url 'sqlite://dev?mode=memory'` with a simple HCL schema (e.g. /workspace/assets/formatted.hcl) — record created file name and EXACT contents; diff again (second file contents, incremental); diff with --to as SQL file; diff with --to sqlite db url; `migrate lint --dev-url ...` on dirs with issues (e.g. drop table, destructive changes) and clean dirs — exact report format; `migrate import` from a goose/dbmate-style dir if feasible (at least --help and basic error behavior). Record exit codes throughout.

SQLITE TYPE MAPPING. Spec file: /workspace/specs/sqlite_types.md. Create sqlite tables via python3 with one column per declared type: INT, INTEGER, TINYINT, SMALLINT, MEDIUMINT, BIGINT, UNSIGNED BIG INT, INT2, INT8, CHARACTER(20), VARCHAR(255), VARYING CHARACTER(20), NCHAR(55), NATIVE CHARACTER(70), NVARCHAR(100), TEXT, CLOB, BLOB, REAL, DOUBLE, DOUBLE PRECISION, FLOAT, NUMERIC, DECIMAL(10,5), BOOLEAN, DATE, DATETIME, TIME, TIMESTAMP, JSON, UUID, and unknown/garbage types like FOO, INT(11), VARCHAR with no size. Run `schema inspect -u sqlite://...` and record the exact HCL `type = ...` rendering for each. Also: integer PK vs INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT rendering; default value rendering (quoted strings with quotes/escapes, negative numbers, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, expressions in parens, NULL default, blob literals); NOT NULL rendering; collate clauses; generated columns; column-level UNIQUE vs unique indexes; table-level constraints (PK, FK with actions, CHECK); STRICT tables if supported. Also record `schema inspect --format '{{ sql . }}'` output for a representative db. Spec must be a complete mapping table.

HCL SCHEMA PARSING & ERRORS. Spec file: /workspace/specs/hcl_schema.md. Investigate how the tool parses Atlas HCL schema files when used as --to for `schema apply`/`schema diff` (with --dev-url sqlite://...?mode=memory as needed). Probe: valid minimal schema (schema + table + columns); the /workspace/assets/formatted.hcl file (has charset/collate attrs — how are they handled for sqlite? error or ignored?); syntax errors (exact parse error output format with line/col); unknown block types; unknown attributes; missing schema reference; duplicate table; type expressions like varchar(255), decimal(10,2), enum?; references column.id, schema.test; index blocks; foreign_key blocks; primary_key blocks; comment handling. Goal: enough to write an HCL parser compatible with these files and to reproduce the exact error messages for malformed input.

MISC ERRORS & FLAG PARSING. Spec file: /workspace/specs/errors_misc.md. Probe general cobra/pflag behavior of the binary: unknown shorthand flag, flag missing value (`--url` at end), `=` vs space in flags, combined shorthands, `--` terminator, help flag on every subcommand position; error message format and exit codes for: required-flag violations (e.g. `schema inspect` with no -u, `schema diff` missing --to), too many args (`schema inspect extra args`), invalid URLs for -u (empty string, 'sqlite://', 'not a url', 'mysql://u:p@nonexistenthost:3306/db' — connection refused exact text), unsupported scheme. Also: does the community-edition notice print on error paths? Env vars like ATLAS_NO_UPDATE_NOTIFIER? Check behavior of `--env` pointing to missing env across several commands. Also `migrate apply` without --url. Record exact stderr/stdout/exit code for each case.

exit=0
'atlas schema inspect' connects to the given database and inspects its schema.
It then prints to the screen the schema of that database in Atlas DDL syntax. This output can be
saved to a file, commonly by redirecting the output to a file named with a ".hcl" suffix:

  atlas schema inspect -u "mysql://user:pass@localhost:3306/dbname" > schema.hcl

This file can then be edited and used with the `atlas schema apply` command to plan
and execute schema migrations against the given database. In cases where users wish to inspect
all multiple schemas in a given database (for instance a MySQL server may contain multiple named
databases), omit the relevant part from the url, e.g. "mysql://user:pass@localhost:3306/".
To select specific schemas from the databases, users may use the "--schema" (or "-s" shorthand)
flag.

Usage:
  atlas schema inspect [flags]

Examples:
  atlas schema inspect -u "mysql://user:pass@localhost:3306/dbname"
  atlas schema inspect -u "mariadb://user:pass@localhost:3306/" --schema=schemaA,schemaB -s schemaC
  atlas schema inspect --url "postgres://user:pass@host:port/dbname?sslmode=disable"
  atlas schema inspect -u "sqlite://file:ex1.db?_fk=1"

Flags:
  -u, --url string        [driver://username:password@address/dbname?param=value] select a resource using the URL format
      --dev-url string    [driver://username:password@address/dbname?param=value] select a dev database using the URL format
  -s, --schema strings    set schema names
      --exclude strings   list of glob patterns used to filter resources from applying
      --format string     Go template to use to format the output
  -h, --help              help for inspect

Global Flags:
  -c, --config string        select config (project) file using URL format (default "file://atlas.hcl")
      --env string           set which env from the config file to use
      --var <name>=<value>   input variables (default [])
---STDERR---

'atlas migrate' wraps several sub-commands for migration management.

Usage:
  atlas migrate [command]

Available Commands:
  apply       Applies pending migration files on the connected database.
  diff        Compute the diff between the migration directory and a desired state and create a new migration file.
  hash        Hash (re-)creates an integrity hash file for the migration directory.
  import      Import a migration directory from another migration management tool to the Atlas format.
  lint        Run analysis on the migration directory
  new         Creates a new empty migration file in the migration directory.
  set         Set the current version of the migration history table.
  status      Get information about the current migration status.
  validate    Validates the migration directories checksum and SQL statements.

Flags:
  -c, --config string        select config (project) file using URL format (default "file://atlas.hcl")
      --env string           set which env from the config file to use
  -h, --help                 help for migrate
      --var <name>=<value>   input variables (default [])

Use "atlas migrate [command] --help" for more information about a command.
---STDERR---

The 'atlas migrate diff' command uses the dev-database to calculate the current state of the migration directory
by executing its files. It then compares its state to the desired state and create a new migration file containing
SQL statements for moving from the current to the desired state. The desired state can be another another database,
an HCL, SQL, or ORM schema. See: https://atlasgo.io/versioned/diff

Usage:
  atlas migrate diff [flags] [name]

Examples:
  atlas migrate diff --dev-url "docker://mysql/8/dev" --to "file://schema.hcl"
  atlas migrate diff --dev-url "docker://postgres/15/dev?search_path=public" --to "file://atlas.hcl" add_users_table
  atlas migrate diff --dev-url "mysql://user:pass@localhost:3306/dev" --to "mysql://user:pass@localhost:3306/dbname"
  atlas migrate diff --env dev --format '{{ sql . "  " }}'

Flags:
      --to strings              [driver://username:password@address/dbname?param=value] select a desired state using the URL format
      --dev-url string          [driver://username:password@address/dbname?param=value] select a dev database using the URL format
      --dir string              select migration directory using URL format (default "file://migrations")
      --dir-format string       select migration file format (default "atlas")
  -s, --schema strings          set schema names
      --lock-timeout duration   set how long to wait for the database lock (default 10s)
      --format string           Go template to use to format the output
      --qualifier string        qualify tables with custom qualifier when working on a single schema
      --edit                    edit the generated migration file(s)
  -h, --help                    help for diff

Global Flags:

import sqlite3, os
for f in ['pk.db','defaults.db','misc.db','constraints.db','strict.db']:
    if os.path.exists(f): os.remove(f)

# pk.db: integer PK vs autoincrement vs non-integer PK vs composite
c = sqlite3.connect('pk.db')
c.execute("CREATE TABLE t_int_pk (id int PRIMARY KEY, name text)")
c.execute("CREATE TABLE t_integer_pk (id integer PRIMARY KEY, name text)")
c.execute("CREATE TABLE t_autoinc (id integer PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, name text)")
c.execute("CREATE TABLE t_text_pk (id text PRIMARY KEY, name text)")
c.execute("CREATE TABLE t_composite (a int, b text, PRIMARY KEY (a, b))")
c.commit(); c.close()

# defaults.db
c = sqlite3.connect('defaults.db')
c.execute("""CREATE TABLE t_defaults (
  c1 text DEFAULT 'hello',
  c2 text DEFAULT 'it''s',
  c3 text DEFAULT 'say "hi"',
  c4 int DEFAULT -5,
  c5 real DEFAULT 3.14,
  c6 text DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  c7 int DEFAULT (1+2),
  c8 text DEFAULT NULL,
  c9 blob DEFAULT x'FF00',
  c10 text DEFAULT 'with\nnewline',
  c11 integer DEFAULT 0,
  c12 text DEFAULT 'back\\slash'
)""")
c.commit(); c.close()

# misc.db: not null, collate, generated columns, unique
c = sqlite3.connect('misc.db')
c.execute("""CREATE TABLE t_misc (
  a text NOT NULL,
  b text COLLATE NOCASE,
  c text NOT NULL COLLATE RTRIM,
  d int GENERATED ALWAYS AS (abs(-1)) VIRTUAL,
  e int GENERATED ALWAYS AS (1*2) STORED
)""")
c.execute("CREATE TABLE t_unique_col (a int UNIQUE, b text)")
c.execute("CREATE TABLE t_unique_idx (a int, b text)")
c.execute("CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_u ON t_unique_idx (a)")
c.execute("CREATE INDEX idx_n ON t_unique_idx (b)")
c.commit(); c.close()

# constraints.db: FK with actions, CHECK
c = sqlite3.connect('constraints.db')
c.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON")
c.execute("CREATE TABLE parent (id integer PRIMARY KEY, code text UNIQUE)")
c.execute("""CREATE TABLE child (
  id integer PRIMARY KEY,
  parent_id int REFERENCES parent(id) ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE SET NULL,
  code text,
  age int CHECK (age >= 0),
  FOREIGN KEY (code) REFERENCES parent(code) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  CONSTRAINT chk_age CHECK (age < 150)
)""")
c.commit(); c.close()

# strict.db
c = sqlite3.connect('strict.db')
try:
    c.execute("CREATE TABLE t_strict (id integer PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL, val real) STRICT")
    c.commit()
    print("strict ok")
except Exception as e:
    print("strict failed:", e)
c.close()
print("done")
EOF

'atlas migrate apply' reads the migration state of the connected database and computes what migrations are pending.
It then attempts to apply the pending migration files in the correct order onto the database. 
The first argument denotes the maximum number of migration files to apply.
As a safety measure 'atlas migrate apply' will abort with an error, if:
  - the migration directory is not in sync with the 'atlas.sum' file
  - the migration and database history do not match each other

  atlas migrate apply [flags] [amount]

--- out:
'atlas schema inspect' connects to the given database and inspects its schema.
It then prints to the screen the schema of that database in Atlas DDL syntax. This output can be
saved to a file, commonly by redirecting the output to a file named with a ".hcl" suffix:

  atlas schema inspect -u "mysql://user:pass@localhost:3306/dbname" > schema.hcl

This file can then be edited and used with the `atlas schema apply` command to plan
and execute schema migrations against the given database. In cases where users wish to inspect
all multiple schemas in a given database (for instance a MySQL server may contain multiple named
databases), omit the relevant part from the url, e.g. "mysql://user:pass@localhost:3306/".
To select specific schemas from the databases, users may use the "--schema" (or "-s" shorthand)
flag.

Usage:
  atlas schema inspect [flags]

Examples:
  atlas schema inspect -u "mysql://user:pass@localhost:3306/dbname"
  atlas schema inspect -u "mariadb://user:pass@localhost:3306/" --schema=schemaA,schemaB -s schemaC
  atlas schema inspect --url "postgres://user:pass@host:port/dbname?sslmode=disable"
  atlas schema inspect -u "sqlite://file:ex1.db?_fk=1"

Flags:
  -u, --url string        [driver://username:password@address/dbname?param=value] select a resource using the URL format
      --dev-url string    [driver://username:password@address/dbname?param=value] select a dev database using the URL format
  -s, --schema strings    set schema names
      --exclude strings   list of glob patterns used to filter resources from applying
      --format string     Go template to use to format the output
  -h, --help              help for inspect

Global Flags:
  -c, --config string        select config (project) file using URL format (default "file://atlas.hcl")
      --env string           set which env from the config file to use
      --var <name>=<value>   input variables (default [])

import sqlite3

def mk(name, ddl):
    import os
    try: os.remove(name)
    except FileNotFoundError: pass
    con = sqlite3.connect(name)
    con.executescript(ddl)
    con.commit(); con.close()

base = '''
CREATE TABLE users (
  id integer PRIMARY KEY,
  name varchar(255) NOT NULL,
  age integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);
'''
mk('mod_base.db', base)
# change type of age integer->bigint
mk('mod_type.db', base.replace('age integer', 'age bigint'))
# change null: name NOT NULL -> NULL
mk('mod_null.db', base.replace('name varchar(255) NOT NULL', 'name varchar(255) NULL'))
# change default: 0 -> 1
mk('mod_default.db', base.replace('DEFAULT 0', 'DEFAULT 1'))
# add index
mk('mod_addidx.db', base + 'CREATE INDEX idx_age ON users (age);\n')
# pk on different column set / drop pk (sqlite: table without pk)
mk('mod_nopk.db', base.replace('id integer PRIMARY KEY', 'id integer'))
# add fk table
mk('mod_fk.db', base + '''
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id integer PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id integer,
  FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users (id)
);
''')
print("done")
EOF
ls mod_*.db

import hashlib, base64
def b64(h): return base64.b64encode(h).decode()
def unb64(s): return base64.b64decode(s)
# two empty files example
n1="20260810060023_myname.sql"; h1=unb64("YL0CKgzWFAV3/MeMKK/BHWA9CJIeTK0i9cRpxTtOC10=")
n2="20260810060024_second one.sql"; h2=unb64("z37r5buvGo8fJ2YbEe8+3srCMxkjqHHk60S7XQLEYEQ=")
target="RoOu15OJLixAZQmtZkD3wTAgnbnaY6mR9siwSKp37yI="
files=[(n1,h1),(n2,h2)]
def sha(d): return hashlib.sha256(d).digest()
cands={}
cands["sha256(concat name+rawhash)"]=b"".join(n.encode()+h for n,h in files)
cands["sha256(concat name+b64hash)"]=b"".join(n.encode()+base64.b64encode(h) for n,h in files)
cands["sha256(concat rawhash+name)"]=b"".join(h+n.encode() for n,h in files)
cands["sha256(concat hexhash+name)"]=b"".join(h.hex().encode()+n.encode() for n,h in files)
cands["sha256(concat line 'name h1:b64\\n')"]=b"".join((f"{n} h1:{b64(h)}\n").encode() for n,h in files)
cands["sha256(concat line 'name h1:b64')"]=b"".join((f"{n} h1:{b64(h)}").encode() for n,h in files)
cands["sha256(concat b64)"]=b"".join(base64.b64encode(h) for n,h in files)
cands["sha256(concat raw)"]=b"".join(h for n,h in files)
cands["sha256(concat 'h1:b64')"]=b"".join(("h1:"+b64(h)).encode() for n,h in files)
cands["sha256(concat hex+'  '+name+'\\n')"]=b"".join(("%s  %s\n"%(h.hex(),n)).encode() for n,h in files)
cands["sha256(concat name+hex)"]=b"".join(n.encode()+h.hex().encode() for n,h in files)
cands["sha256(concat name+'\\n'+raw)"]=b"".join(n.encode()+b"\n"+h for n,h in files)
for k,d in cands.items():
    r=b64(sha(d))
    print(("MATCH " if r==target else "      ")+k, r)
EOF

args.command:
python3 - <<'EOF'
import hashlib, base64, os
d="/tmp/probe/p5/migrations"
files=sorted(f for f in os.listdir(d) if f.endswith(".sql") and os.path.isfile(os.path.join(d,f)))
lines=[]
total=hashlib.sha256()
for n in files:
    c=open(os.path.join(d,n),'rb').read()
    fh=hashlib.sha256(n.encode()+c).digest()
    fb=base64.b64encode(fh).decode()
    lines.append(f"{n} h1:{fb}")
    total.update(n.encode()+fb.encode())
out="h1:"+base64.b64encode(total.digest()).decode()+"\n"+"\n".join(lines)+"\n"
actual=open(os.path.join(d,"atlas.sum"),'rb').read().decode()
print("EXACT MATCH" if out==actual else "MISMATCH")
print(repr(out))
EOF

args.content:
# `atlas schema fmt` — Behavioral Spec

Binary probed: `/tmp/atlas_orig` (atlas community edition, unofficial dev build).
All probes run with stdout/stderr separated (`cmd >out 2>err; echo $?`), piped (non-TTY) unless noted.
Probe scratch dir: `/tmp/probe`. Probing user was `root`.

## Summary of behavior

- Rewrites files **in place**; never prints formatted content to stdout.
- Prints to **stdout** the path of each file it actually changed, one per line (path exactly as constructed from the argument, see "Path echoing"). Files already in canonical form produce no output and are **not rewritten** (mtime untouched).
- Exit code `0` on success (even for malformed HCL); exit code `1` with `Error: ...` on stderr for stat/flag errors.
- Formatting style is canonical `hclwrite.Format` (hashicorp/hcl/v2): token-based, tolerant of syntax errors, preserves comments, heredocs, line-ending style (CRLF kept), and does not add a missing trailing newline.
- With no path args, formats `.hcl` files in the **current directory** (non-recursive). Directory args are also **non-recursive**.
- Only files whose name ends in lowercase `.hcl` are considered. `.HCL`, `.txt`, extensionless files are silently skipped — even when passed explicitly as arguments.
- Hidden files (`*.hcl` dotfiles) **are** processed.
- Symlinks to `.hcl` files are followed; the target is rewritten, the link name is printed.
- Global flags (`-c/--config`, `--env`, `--var`) are accepted but have no observable effect; no `atlas.hcl` config file is required or consulted.

## `schema fmt --help` (verbatim)

Command: `/tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt --help`
Exit code: `0`. stdout below (stderr empty). `-h` produces identical output. `--help` wins over extra args (`schema fmt --help extra` → exit 0, prints help).

```
'atlas schema fmt' formats all ".hcl" files under the given paths using
canonical HCL layout style as defined by the github.com/hashicorp/hcl/v2/hclwrite package.
Unless stated otherwise, the fmt command will use the current directory.

After running, the command will print the names of the files it has formatted. If all
files in the directory are formatted, no input will be printed out.

Usage:
  atlas schema fmt [path ...] [flags]

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for fmt

Global Flags:
  -c, --config string        select config (project) file using URL format (default "file://atlas.hcl")
      --env string           set which env from the config file to use
      --var <name>=<value>   input variables (default [])
```

(Trailing newline after the last line; no trailing blank line.)

## No arguments

### Empty directory (no `.hcl` files)

Command (cwd = empty dir): `/tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt`
Exit code: `0`. stdout empty, stderr empty.

### Directory with `.hcl` files

cwd contained `a.hcl` (copy of `assets/unformatted.hcl`) and `b.hcl` (copy of `assets/formatted.hcl`).

Command: `/tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt`
Exit code: `0`. stderr empty. stdout:

```
a.hcl
```

- Only the unformatted file is listed, bare filename (no `./` prefix).
- `a.hcl` was rewritten in place to be byte-identical to `assets/formatted.hcl`.
- `b.hcl` untouched (byte-identical, mtime unchanged).
- Piped stdin is ignored in no-arg mode: `echo 'x = 1' | atlas schema fmt` in a dir with an unformatted file behaved exactly as plain `atlas schema fmt` (formatted the cwd file, exit 0).

## Single file argument

Command: `/tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt single/u.hcl` (u.hcl = unformatted.hcl)
Exit code: `0`. stderr empty. stdout:

```
single/u.hcl
```

File rewritten to byte-identical `assets/formatted.hcl`.

Command: `/tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt /workspace/assets/formatted.hcl` (already formatted)
Exit code: `0`. stdout empty, stderr empty. File untouched.

### Non-`.hcl` file passed explicitly

Command: `/tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt noext.txt` (copy of unformatted.hcl)
Exit code: `0`. stdout empty, stderr empty. File **unchanged** — silently skipped, not an error.

### Empty `.hcl` file

`touch emptyfile.hcl; atlas schema fmt emptyfile.hcl` → exit 0, no output, file stays 0 bytes.

### Duplicate argument

`atlas schema fmt dup.hcl dup.hcl` (unformatted) → exit 0, stdout `dup.hcl` once (second pass finds it already formatted).

## Multiple file arguments

Command: `/tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt multi/z.hcl multi/m.hcl /workspace/assets/formatted.hcl`
(z.hcl, m.hcl unformatted)
Exit code: `0`. stderr empty. stdout — **argument order preserved** (not sorted):

```
multi/z.hcl
multi/m.hcl
```

## Directory argument

`dirarg/` contained `top.hcl` (unformatted), `sub/nested.hcl` (unformatted), `readme.txt`, `UPPER.HCL` (unformatted copy).

Command: `/tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt dirarg`
Exit code: `0`. stderr empty. stdout:

```
dirarg/top.hcl
```

- **Non-recursive**: `sub/nested.hcl` left unchanged.
- Case-sensitive extension: `UPPER.HCL` unchanged.
- Non-`.hcl` files ignored.
- Entries processed in **alphabetical order**: a dir with unformatted `c.hcl b.hcl a.hcl` printed `order/a.hcl`, `order/b.hcl`, `order/c.hcl`.
- Hidden files are processed: a dir containing `.hidden.hcl` (unformatted) printed `hdir/.hidden.hcl`.
- Trailing slash on the arg is cleaned: `atlas schema fmt dotdir/` printed `dotdir/trail.hcl` (single slash).
- `atlas schema fmt .` from inside a dir printed bare `d.hcl` (no `./` prefix), same as no-arg mode.
- Absolute dir arg: `atlas schema fmt /tmp/probe/dotdir` printed `/tmp/probe/dotdir/d.hcl`.
- Empty directory arg → exit 0, no output.
- A directory whose name ends in `.hcl` (`weird.hcl/`) → treated as a directory, exit 0, no output.

## Path echoing rules

The printed path is the argument joined with the filename:

- explicit file arg → printed verbatim as given (`single/u.hcl`, `/tmp/probe/dotdir/abs.hcl`)
- dir arg → `<arg>/<name>` with path cleaned (no double slash, `.` → bare name)
- no args (cwd) → bare `<name>`

## Error cases

### Nonexistent path

Command: `/tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt nonexistent.hcl`
Exit code: `1`. stdout empty. stderr (exactly one line, trailing newline):

```
Error: stat nonexistent.hcl: no such file or directory
```

Empty-string arg: `atlas schema fmt ""` → exit 1, stderr `Error: stat : no such file or directory`.

### Partial application on error

Args are processed in order; files before the failing one are formatted and printed, then processing stops:

Command: `/tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt partial.hcl nonexistent.hcl`
Exit code: `1`. stdout: `partial.hcl` (file was formatted). stderr: `Error: stat nonexistent.hcl: no such file or directory`.

If the bad path comes first, nothing is processed: `atlas schema fmt nonexistent.hcl /workspace/assets/unformatted.hcl` → exit 1, stdout empty, same error.

### `-` (stdin) not supported

Command: `cat unformatted.hcl | /tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt -`
Exit code: `1`. stdout empty. stderr:

```
Error: stat -: no such file or directory
```

`-` is treated as a literal filename; there is no stdin mode.

### Unknown flag

Command: `/tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt --badflag`
Exit code: `1`. stdout empty. stderr (single line; **no usage text printed**):

```
Error: unknown flag: --badflag
```

## Malformed HCL

Command: `/tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt bad.hcl` (copy of `assets/malformed_config.hcl`)
Exit code: **`0`** (no parse error!). stderr empty. stdout: `bad.hcl`.

Input (`assets/malformed_config.hcl`):

```
env "bad" {
  url = "sqlite://test.db"
  invalid syntax here {{
}
```

File after formatting (note: `{{` split, final `}` re-indented; still invalid HCL):

```
env "bad" {
  url = "sqlite://test.db"
  invalid syntax here { {
    }
```

The formatter is token-based (hclwrite) and does not validate syntax; it reformats whatever token stream it sees.

## Formatting semantics (canonical hclwrite style)

Observed on a synthetic file covering comments, alignment, lists, function calls, heredocs.

Input:

```
# leading comment
// another comment style
schema "test" { # inline comment on block
  charset = "utf8mb4" # inline attr comment
  x   =   1
  longer_name = 2
  list = [1,  2,    3]
  nested_list = [
    "a",
    "b",
  ]
  val = func("a",  1 , true)
  heredoc = <<EOT
  hello   world
  indented   more
EOT
  after = "kept"
}
/* block
   comment */
block   "a"   "b"   {
  /* inline block comment */ y = 1
}
```

Output (exit 0, filename printed):

```
# leading comment
// another comment style
schema "test" {           # inline comment on block
  charset     = "utf8mb4" # inline attr comment
  x           = 1
  longer_name = 2
  list        = [1, 2, 3]
  nested_list = [
    "a",
    "b",
  ]
  val     = func("a", 1, true)
  heredoc = <<EOT
  hello   world
  indented   more
EOT
  after   = "kept"
}
/* block
   comment */
block "a" "b" {
  /* inline block comment */ y = 1
}
```

Rules observed:

- Multiple spaces between block name/labels/`{` collapse to one: `block   "a"   "b"   {` → `block "a" "b" {`.
- `=` of consecutive attributes in the same group are aligned (padded) to the longest name; alignment groups are broken by heredocs, comments-with-content lines behave per hclwrite rules.
- Trailing inline comments on consecutive lines are column-aligned (`# inline comment on block` padded to align with `# inline attr comment`).
- Spaces around `=` normalized to exactly one each side (plus alignment padding).
- Lists: `[1,  2,    3]` → `[1, 2, 3]`; multi-line list layout preserved (one item per line kept).
- Function calls: `func("a",  1 , true)` → `func("a", 1, true)`.
- Heredocs: marker and **body preserved verbatim** (inner spacing untouched); heredoc breaks the `=` alignment group.
- Comments (`#`, `//`, `/* */`) preserved, including block comments spanning lines; standalone comment lines not re-indented beyond their column.
- Blank lines preserved, including multiple trailing blank lines at EOF (a file `x = 1\n\n\n\n` is considered already formatted — not listed, not rewritten).

### Line endings and EOF newline

- **CRLF preserved**: input `x = 1\r\ny    =    2\r\n` → output `x = 1\r\ny = 2\r\n` (spacing fixed, `\r\n` kept).
- **No trailing newline added**: file containing exactly `x = 1` (no `\n`) is considered already formatted — not listed, not rewritten.

## File metadata / write behavior

- Already-formatted files are **not rewritten**: mtime unchanged after running fmt on them (verified with `stat -c %Y` before/after).
- Rewritten files **keep their permission bits** (640 stayed 640).
- Read-only file (mode 444) was still formatted successfully — but the probe ran as `root`, so this may fail for unprivileged users; reimplementation should expect a write error to surface as `Error: ...` on stderr with exit 1 (not directly observed).
- Symlink arg (`link.hcl` → `linktarget.hcl`): target rewritten in place, stdout printed the **link name** `link.hcl`, exit 0.

## TTY vs piped

Command under pseudo-TTY: `script -qec '/tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt ttydir/t.hcl' /dev/null`
Exit code: `0`. Output identical to piped mode except line endings appear as `\r\n` (pty driver artifact): `ttydir/t.hcl\r\n`. No prompts, spinners, colors, or other TTY-dependent behavior.

## Global flags

`atlas schema fmt --env foo withfiles` → exit 0, normal behavior. No `atlas.hcl` was present in any probe directory; fmt never complained about a missing config file. `-c/--config`, `--var` were not observed to alter behavior.

## Reimplementation checklist

1. Args: zero or more paths; default `["."]`.
2. For each arg in order: `os.Stat`; on failure print `Error: stat <arg>: no such file or directory` (Go `os.Stat` error text) to stderr, exit 1, stop processing further args.
3. If arg is a dir: list entries (alphabetical), take only regular entries ending in `.hcl` (lowercase), non-recursive, dotfiles included; join paths with `filepath.Join` semantics (`.` → bare name).
4. If arg is a file: process only if name ends in `.hcl`; else skip silently.
5. For each candidate: read bytes, run `hclwrite.Format`, compare; if different, write back (preserving mode) and print the path + `\n` to stdout.
6. Unknown flags: `Error: unknown flag: --<name>` on stderr, exit 1, no usage text.
7. Exit 0 otherwise. Never print formatted content; never read stdin.

display.content:
# `atlas schema fmt` — Behavioral Spec

Binary probed: `/tmp/atlas_orig` (atlas community edition, unofficial dev build).
All probes run with stdout/stderr separated (`cmd >out 2>err; echo $?`), piped (non-TTY) unless noted.
Probe scratch dir: `/tmp/probe`. Probing user was `root`.

## Summary of behavior

- Rewrites files **in place**; never prints formatted content to stdout.
- Prints to **stdout** the path of each file it actually changed, one per line (path exactly as constructed from the argument, see "Path echoing"). Files already in canonical form produce no output and are **not rewritten** (mtime untouched).
- Exit code `0` on success (even for malformed HCL); exit code `1` with `Error: ...` on stderr for stat/flag errors.
- Formatting style is canonical `hclwrite.Format` (hashicorp/hcl/v2): token-based, tolerant of syntax errors, preserves comments, heredocs, line-ending style (CRLF kept), and does not add a missing trailing newline.
- With no path args, formats `.hcl` files in the **current directory** (non-recursive). Directory args are also **non-recursive**.
- Only files whose name ends in lowercase `.hcl` are considered. `.HCL`, `.txt`, extensionless files are silently skipped — even when passed explicitly as arguments.
- Hidden files (`*.hcl` dotfiles) **are** processed.
- Symlinks to `.hcl` files are followed; the target is rewritten, the link name is printed.
- Global flags (`-c/--config`, `--env`, `--var`) are accepted but have no observable effect; no `atlas.hcl` config file is required or consulted.

## `schema fmt --help` (verbatim)

Command: `/tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt --help`
Exit code: `0`. stdout below (stderr empty). `-h` produces identical output. `--help` wins over extra args (`schema fmt --help extra` → exit 0, prints help).

```
'atlas schema fmt' formats all ".hcl" files under the given paths using
canonical HCL layout style as defined by the github.com/hashicorp/hcl/v2/hclwrite package.
Unless stated otherwise, the fmt command will use the current directory.

After running, the command will print the names of the files it has formatted. If all
files in the directory are formatted, no input will be printed out.

Usage:
  atlas schema fmt [path ...] [flags]

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for fmt

Global Flags:
  -c, --config string        select config (project) file using URL format (default "file://atlas.hcl")
      --env string           set which env from the config file to use
      --var <name>=<value>   input variables (default [])
```

(Trailing newline after the last line; no trailing blank line.)

## No arguments

### Empty directory (no `.hcl` files)

Command (cwd = empty dir): `/tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt`
Exit code: `0`. stdout empty, stderr empty.

### Directory with `.hcl` files

cwd contained `a.hcl` (copy of `assets/unformatted.hcl`) and `b.hcl` (copy of `assets/formatted.hcl`).

Command: `/tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt`
Exit code: `0`. stderr empty. stdout:

```
a.hcl
```

- Only the unformatted file is listed, bare filename (no `./` prefix).
- `a.hcl` was rewritten in place to be byte-identical to `assets/formatted.hcl`.
- `b.hcl` untouched (byte-identical, mtime unchanged).
- Piped stdin is ignored in no-arg mode: `echo 'x = 1' | atlas schema fmt` in a dir with an unformatted file behaved exactly as plain `atlas schema fmt` (formatted the cwd file, exit 0).

## Single file argument

Command: `/tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt single/u.hcl` (u.hcl = unformatted.hcl)
Exit code: `0`. stderr empty. stdout:

```
single/u.hcl
```

File rewritten to byte-identical `assets/formatted.hcl`.

Command: `/tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt /workspace/assets/formatted.hcl` (already formatted)
Exit code: `0`. stdout empty, stderr empty. File untouched.

### Non-`.hcl` file passed explicitly

Command: `/tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt noext.txt` (copy of unformatted.hcl)
Exit code: `0`. stdout empty, stderr empty. File **unchanged** — silently skipped, not an error.

### Empty `.hcl` file

`touch emptyfile.hcl; atlas schema fmt emptyfile.hcl` → exit 0, no output, file stays 0 bytes.

### Duplicate argument

`atlas schema fmt dup.hcl dup.hcl` (unformatted) → exit 0, stdout `dup.hcl` once (second pass finds it already formatted).

## Multiple file arguments

Command: `/tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt multi/z.hcl multi/m.hcl /workspace/assets/formatted.hcl`
(z.hcl, m.hcl unformatted)
Exit code: `0`. stderr empty. stdout — **argument order preserved** (not sorted):

```
multi/z.hcl
multi/m.hcl
```

## Directory argument

`dirarg/` contained `top.hcl` (unformatted), `sub/nested.hcl` (unformatted), `readme.txt`, `UPPER.HCL` (unformatted copy).

Command: `/tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt dirarg`
Exit code: `0`. stderr empty. stdout:

```
dirarg/top.hcl
```

- **Non-recursive**: `sub/nested.hcl` left unchanged.
- Case-sensitive extension: `UPPER.HCL` unchanged.
- Non-`.hcl` files ignored.
- Entries processed in **alphabetical order**: a dir with unformatted `c.hcl b.hcl a.hcl` printed `order/a.hcl`, `order/b.hcl`, `order/c.hcl`.
- Hidden files are processed: a dir containing `.hidden.hcl` (unformatted) printed `hdir/.hidden.hcl`.
- Trailing slash on the arg is cleaned: `atlas schema fmt dotdir/` printed `dotdir/trail.hcl` (single slash).
- `atlas schema fmt .` from inside a dir printed bare `d.hcl` (no `./` prefix), same as no-arg mode.
- Absolute dir arg: `atlas schema fmt /tmp/probe/dotdir` printed `/tmp/probe/dotdir/d.hcl`.
- Empty directory arg → exit 0, no output.
- A directory whose name ends in `.hcl` (`weird.hcl/`) → treated as a directory, exit 0, no output.

## Path echoing rules

The printed path is the argument joined with the filename:

- explicit file arg → printed verbatim as given (`single/u.hcl`, `/tmp/probe/dotdir/abs.hcl`)
- dir arg → `<arg>/<name>` with path cleaned (no double slash, `.` → bare name)
- no args (cwd) → bare `<name>`

## Error cases

### Nonexistent path

Command: `/tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt nonexistent.hcl`
Exit code: `1`. stdout empty. stderr (exactly one line, trailing newline):

```
Error: stat nonexistent.hcl: no such file or directory
```

Empty-string arg: `atlas schema fmt ""` → exit 1, stderr `Error: stat : no such file or directory`.

### Partial application on error

Args are processed in order; files before the failing one are formatted and printed, then processing stops:

Command: `/tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt partial.hcl nonexistent.hcl`
Exit code: `1`. stdout: `partial.hcl` (file was formatted). stderr: `Error: stat nonexistent.hcl: no such file or directory`.

If the bad path comes first, nothing is processed: `atlas schema fmt nonexistent.hcl /workspace/assets/unformatted.hcl` → exit 1, stdout empty, same error.

### `-` (stdin) not supported

Command: `cat unformatted.hcl | /tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt -`
Exit code: `1`. stdout empty. stderr:

```
Error: stat -: no such file or directory
```

`-` is treated as a literal filename; there is no stdin mode.

### Unknown flag

Command: `/tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt --badflag`
Exit code: `1`. stdout empty. stderr (single line; **no usage text printed**):

```
Error: unknown flag: --badflag
```

## Malformed HCL

Command: `/tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt bad.hcl` (copy of `assets/malformed_config.hcl`)
Exit code: **`0`** (no parse error!). stderr empty. stdout: `bad.hcl`.

Input (`assets/malformed_config.hcl`):

```
env "bad" {
  url = "sqlite://test.db"
  invalid syntax here {{
}
```

File after formatting (note: `{{` split, final `}` re-indented; still invalid HCL):

```
env "bad" {
  url = "sqlite://test.db"
  invalid syntax here { {
    }
```

The formatter is token-based (hclwrite) and does not validate syntax; it reformats whatever token stream it sees.

## Formatting semantics (canonical hclwrite style)

Observed on a synthetic file covering comments, alignment, lists, function calls, heredocs.

Input:

```
# leading comment
// another comment style
schema "test" { # inline comment on block
  charset = "utf8mb4" # inline attr comment
  x   =   1
  longer_name = 2
  list = [1,  2,    3]
  nested_list = [
    "a",
    "b",
  ]
  val = func("a",  1 , true)
  heredoc = <<EOT
  hello   world
  indented   more
EOT
  after = "kept"
}
/* block
   comment */
block   "a"   "b"   {
  /* inline block comment */ y = 1
}
```

Output (exit 0, filename printed):

```
# leading comment
// another comment style
schema "test" {           # inline comment on block
  charset     = "utf8mb4" # inline attr comment
  x           = 1
  longer_name = 2
  list        = [1, 2, 3]
  nested_list = [
    "a",
    "b",
  ]
  val     = func("a", 1, true)
  heredoc = <<EOT
  hello   world
  indented   more
EOT
  after   = "kept"
}
/* block
   comment */
block "a" "b" {
  /* inline block comment */ y = 1
}
```

Rules observed:

- Multiple spaces between block name/labels/`{` collapse to one: `block   "a"   "b"   {` → `block "a" "b" {`.
- `=` of consecutive attributes in the same group are aligned (padded) to the longest name; alignment groups are broken by heredocs, comments-with-content lines behave per hclwrite rules.
- Trailing inline comments on consecutive lines are column-aligned (`# inline comment on block` padded to align with `# inline attr comment`).
- Spaces around `=` normalized to exactly one each side (plus alignment padding).
- Lists: `[1,  2,    3]` → `[1, 2, 3]`; multi-line list layout preserved (one item per line kept).
- Function calls: `func("a",  1 , true)` → `func("a", 1, true)`.
- Heredocs: marker and **body preserved verbatim** (inner spacing untouched); heredoc breaks the `=` alignment group.
- Comments (`#`, `//`, `/* */`) preserved, including block comments spanning lines; standalone comment lines not re-indented beyond their column.
- Blank lines preserved, including multiple trailing blank lines at EOF (a file `x = 1\n\n\n\n` is considered already formatted — not listed, not rewritten).

### Line endings and EOF newline

- **CRLF preserved**: input `x = 1\r\ny    =    2\r\n` → output `x = 1\r\ny = 2\r\n` (spacing fixed, `\r\n` kept).
- **No trailing newline added**: file containing exactly `x = 1` (no `\n`) is considered already formatted — not listed, not rewritten.

## File metadata / write behavior

- Already-formatted files are **not rewritten**: mtime unchanged after running fmt on them (verified with `stat -c %Y` before/after).
- Rewritten files **keep their permission bits** (640 stayed 640).
- Read-only file (mode 444) was still formatted successfully — but the probe ran as `root`, so this may fail for unprivileged users; reimplementation should expect a write error to surface as `Error: ...` on stderr with exit 1 (not directly observed).
- Symlink arg (`link.hcl` → `linktarget.hcl`): target rewritten in place, stdout printed the **link name** `link.hcl`, exit 0.

## TTY vs piped

Command under pseudo-TTY: `script -qec '/tmp/atlas_orig schema fmt ttydir/t.hcl' /dev/null`
Exit code: `0`. Output identical to piped mode except line endings appear as `\r\n` (pty driver artifact): `ttydir/t.hcl\r\n`. No prompts, spinners, colors, or other TTY-dependent behavior.

## Global flags

`atlas schema fmt --env foo withfiles` → exit 0, normal behavior. No `atlas.hcl` was present in any probe directory; fmt never complained about a missing config file. `-c/--config`, `--var` were not observed to alter behavior.

## Reimplementation checklist

1. Args: zero or more paths; default `["."]`.
2. For each arg in order: `os.Stat`; on failure print `Error: stat <arg>: no such file or directory` (Go `os.Stat` error text) to stderr, exit 1, stop processing further args.
3. If arg is a dir: list entries (alphabetical), take only regular entries ending in `.hcl` (lowercase), non-recursive, dotfiles included; join paths with `filepath.Join` semantics (`.` → bare name).
4. If arg is a file: process only if name ends in `.hcl`; else skip silently.
5. For each candidate: read bytes, run `hclwrite.Format`, compare; if different, write back (preserving mode) and print the path + `\n` to stdout.
6. Unknown flags: `Error: unknown flag: --<name>` on stderr, exit 1, no usage text.
7. Exit 0 otherwise. Never print formatted content; never read stdin.

payload.resultSummary:
Spec written to `/workspace/specs/schema_fmt.md`. Key findings:

1. **In-place rewrite, never stdout**: `schema fmt` rewrites files and prints only the *paths of files it changed* (one per line) to stdout; already-canonical files are not rewritten (mtime untouched) and produce no output.
2. **Token-based, parse-tolerant**: malformed HCL exits 0 and gets "formatted" anyway (canonical `hclwrite.Format`); comments, heredoc bodies, blank lines, CRLF endings are preserved, `=` and trailing comments are column-aligned, and no trailing newline is added if missing.
3. **Non-recursive, lowercase `.hcl` only**: directory args scan just the top level in alphabetical order; `.HCL`/`.txt` files are silently skipped even when passed explicitly; hidden `.hcl` files are included; symlinks are followed (target rewritten, link name printed).
4. **Error model**: nonexistent path → `Error: stat <path>: no such file or directory` on stderr, exit 1, with partial application (earlier args already formatted); `-` is treated as a literal filename (no stdin mode); unknown flags give `Error: unknown flag: --x` with no usage text.
5. **No TTY-dependent behavior** (only pty `\r\n` artifacts), and global flags (`--config`, `--env`, `--var`) are accepted but inert — no `atlas.hcl` required.

args.content:
# Atlas CLI — Top-Level Commands Spec

Binary probed: `/tmp/atlas_orig` ("atlas" database-schema tool, community edition, unofficial dev build).
All outputs captured non-TTY (piped/redirected). Where TTY behavior was suspected, output was also captured under a pseudo-TTY (`script -qec '...' /dev/null`); **no differences** were found for any command in this scope — no ANSI escapes, no prompts, no spinners, no color. All commands in this scope behave identically on TTY and non-TTY.

General conventions observed:

- The binary name in all usage/help/error text is `atlas`.
- All help/usage text goes to **stdout**, exit code `0`.
- All error messages go to **stderr** only (stdout empty on errors), exit code `1`.
- Errors print only the `Error: ...` line(s); usage text is NOT re-printed on errors (i.e. `SilenceUsage` behavior), except that unknown root commands append `Run 'atlas --help' for usage.`.
- All captured outputs end with a single trailing `\n`.
- Root command has **no** `--version` flag; `atlas --version` is an error.
- The root command has no `-v` shorthand; `atlas -v` errors with `unknown shorthand flag`.
- Commands are matched case-sensitively, but unknown-command suggestions are case-insensitive (e.g. `VERSION` suggests `version`).

---

## `atlas` (no args) / `--help` / `-h` / `help`

All four invocations produce byte-identical output on **stdout**, exit code `0`, empty stderr:

- `atlas`
- `atlas --help`
- `atlas -h`
- `atlas help`

Exact stdout (484 bytes, trailing newline included):

```
Manage your database schema as code

Usage:
  atlas [command]

Available Commands:
  completion  Generate the autocompletion script for the specified shell
  help        Help about any command
  license     Display license information
  migrate     Manage versioned migration files
  schema      Work with atlas schemas.
  version     Prints this Atlas CLI version information.

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for atlas

Use "atlas [command] --help" for more information about a command.
```

Extra positional args with `--help` are ignored: `atlas --help extra` prints the same root help, exit `0`.

---

## `atlas help <topic>`

### `atlas help help` / `atlas help --help`

Byte-identical, stdout, exit `0`:

```
Help provides help for any command in the application.
Simply type atlas help [path to command] for full details.

Usage:
  atlas help [command] [flags]

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for help
```

### `atlas help schema`

Identical to `atlas schema --help` and to `atlas schema` (no args). Stdout, exit `0`:

```
The `atlas schema` command groups subcommands working with declarative Atlas schemas.

Usage:
  atlas schema [command]

Available Commands:
  apply       Apply an atlas schema to a target database.
  clean       Removes all objects from the connected database.
  diff        Calculate and print the diff between two schemas.
  fmt         Formats Atlas HCL files
  inspect     Inspect a database and print its schema in Atlas DDL syntax.

Flags:
  -c, --config string        select config (project) file using URL format (default "file://atlas.hcl")
      --env string           set which env from the config file to use
  -h, --help                 help for schema
      --var <name>=<value>   input variables (default [])

Use "atlas schema [command] --help" for more information about a command.
```

Note: backticks in the first line are literal. `fmt` description has no trailing period; `inspect` ends with a period.

### `atlas help migrate`

Identical to `atlas migrate --help` and to `atlas migrate` (no args). Stdout, exit `0`:

```
'atlas migrate' wraps several sub-commands for migration management.

Usage:
  atlas migrate [command]

Available Commands:
  apply       Applies pending migration files on the connected database.
  diff        Compute the diff between the migration directory and a desired state and create a new migration file.
  hash        Hash (re-)creates an integrity hash file for the migration directory.
  import      Import a migration directory from another migration management tool to the Atlas format.
  lint        Run analysis on the migration directory
  new         Creates a new empty migration file in the migration directory.
  set         Set the current version of the migration history table.
  status      Get information about the current migration status.
  validate    Validates the migration directories checksum and SQL statements.

Flags:
  -c, --config string        select config (project) file using URL format (default "file://atlas.hcl")
      --env string           set which env from the config file to use
  -h, --help                 help for migrate
      --var <name>=<value>   input variables (default [])

Use "atlas migrate [command] --help" for more information about a command.
```

Note: single quotes in the first line are literal. `lint` description has no trailing period.

### `atlas help migrate apply`

Stdout, exit `0` (note trailing space at end of line 2, reproduced as-is between `database. ` and newline):

```
'atlas migrate apply' reads the migration state of the connected database and computes what migrations are pending.
It then attempts to apply the pending migration files in the correct order onto the database. 
The first argument denotes the maximum number of migration files to apply.
As a safety measure 'atlas migrate apply' will abort with an error, if:
  - the migration directory is not in sync with the 'atlas.sum' file
  - the migration and database history do not match each other

If run with the "--dry-run" flag, atlas will not execute any SQL.

Usage:
  atlas migrate apply [flags] [amount]

Examples:
  atlas migrate apply -u "mysql://user:pass@localhost:3306/dbname"
  atlas migrate apply --dir "file:///path/to/migration/directory" --url "mysql://user:pass@localhost:3306/dbname" 1
  atlas migrate apply --env dev 1
